The potential minimum is at {{Math|1=''r'' {{=}} ''r''<sub>min</sub> = 2<sup>1/6</sup>σ}}.]]
{{Computational physics}}

In [[computational chemistry]], [[molecular physics]], and [[physical chemistry]], the '''Lennard-Jones potential'''<!-- (Hyphen, not dash. John Lennard-Jones is one person.) --> (also termed the '''LJ potential''' or '''12-6 potential'''; named for [[John Lennard-Jones]]) is an intermolecular [[pair potential]]. Out of all the [[interatomic potential|intermolecular potentials]], the Lennard-Jones potential is probably the one that has been the most extensively studied.<ref name="FischerWendland"/><ref name="Lenhard-2024">{{Cite journal |last1=Lenhard |first1=Johannes |last2=Stephan |first2=Simon |last3=Hasse |first3=Hans |date=2024-05-16 |title=On the History of the Lennard-Jones Potential |journal=Annalen der Physik |volume=536 |issue=6 |language=en |doi=10.1002/andp.202400115 |issn=0003-3804|doi-access=free }}</ref> It is considered an archetype model for simple yet realistic [[intermolecular interaction]]s. The Lennard-Jones potential is often used as a building block in [[molecular modelling|molecular models]] (a.k.a. [[force field (chemistry)|force fields]]) for more complex substances.<ref name="SchwerdtfegerWales">{{Cite journal |last1=Schwerdtfeger |first1=Peter |last2=Wales |first2=David J. |date=2024-04-26 |title=100 Years of the Lennard-Jones Potential |url=https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/acs.jctc.4c00135 |journal=Journal of Chemical Theory and Computation |volume=20 |issue=9 |pages=3379–3405 |language=en |doi=10.1021/acs.jctc.4c00135 |pmid=38669689 |issn=1549-9618|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Many studies of the idealized "Lennard-Jones substance" use the potential to understand the physical nature of matter.

== Overview ==
The Lennard-Jones potential is a simple model that still manages to describe the essential features of interactions between simple atoms and molecules: two interacting particles repel each other at very close distances, attract each other at moderate distances, and eventually stop interacting at infinite distance, as shown in the figure. The Lennard-Jones potential is a pair potential, i.e. no three- or multi-body interactions are covered by the potential.<ref name="SchwerdtfegerWales"/><ref>{{Cite book |last=Stone |first=A. J. |title=The theory of intermolecular forces |date=2016 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0-19-878915-4 |edition=Second edition published in paperback |location=Oxford}}</ref>

The widely used Lennard-Jones 12-6 potential is:<ref name=WhenToUse>{{Cite journal |last1=Wang |first1=Xipeng |last2=Ramírez-Hinestrosa |first2=Simón |last3=Dobnikar |first3=Jure |last4=Frenkel |first4=Daan |date=2020 |title=The Lennard-Jones potential: when (not) to use it |url=https://xlink.rsc.org/?DOI=C9CP05445F |journal=Physical Chemistry Chemical Physics |language=en |volume=22 |issue=19 |pages=10624–10633 |doi=10.1039/C9CP05445F |pmid=31681941 |issn=1463-9076|arxiv=1910.05746 |bibcode=2020PCCP...2210624W }}</ref>
<math display="block">V_\text{LJ}(r) = 4\varepsilon \left[ \left(\frac{\sigma}{r}\right)^{12} - \left(\frac{\sigma}{r}\right)^6 \right] ,</math>
where {{mvar|r}} is the distance between two interacting particles, {{mvar|ε}} is the depth of the [[potential well]], and {{mvar|σ}} is the distance at which the particle-particle potential energy {{mvar|V}} is zero. The Lennard-Jones 12-6 potential has its minimum at a distance of <math>r=r_{\rm min}= 2^{1/6}\sigma,</math> where the potential energy has the value <math>V=-\varepsilon.</math>

The Lennard-Jones potential is usually the standard choice for the development of theories for [[phase (matter)|matter]] (especially soft-matter) as well as for the development and testing of computational methods and algorithms.

Numerous [[interatomic potential|intermolecular potentials]] have been proposed in the past for the modeling of simple soft repulsive and attractive interactions between spherically symmetric particles, i.e. the general shape shown in the Figure. Examples for other potentials are the [[Morse potential]], the [[Mie potential]],<ref name="Mie-1903">{{cite journal |last=Mie |first=Gustav |date=1903 |title=Zur kinetischen Theorie der einatomigen Körper |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1002/andp.19033160802 |journal=Annalen der Physik |language=de |volume=316 |issue=8 |pages=657–697 |bibcode=1903AnP...316..657M |doi=10.1002/andp.19033160802}}</ref> the [[Buckingham potential]] and the Tang-Tönnies potential.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Tang |first1=K. T. |last2=Toennies |first2=J. Peter |date=1984-04-15 |title=An improved simple model for the van der Waals potential based on universal damping functions for the dispersion coefficients |url=https://aip.scitation.org/doi/10.1063/1.447150 |journal=The Journal of Chemical Physics |language=en |volume=80 |issue=8 |pages=3726–3741 |bibcode=1984JChPh..80.3726T |doi=10.1063/1.447150 |issn=0021-9606|url-access=subscription }}</ref> While some of these may be more suited to modelling [[Fluid|real fluids]],<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Lafitte |first1=Thomas |last2=Apostolakou |first2=Anastasia |last3=Avendaño |first3=Carlos |last4=Galindo |first4=Amparo |last5=Adjiman |first5=Claire S. |last6=Müller |first6=Erich A. |last7=Jackson |first7=George |date=2013-10-21 |title=Accurate statistical associating fluid theory for chain molecules formed from Mie segments |journal=The Journal of Chemical Physics |language=en |volume=139 |issue=15 |bibcode=2013JChPh.139o4504L |doi=10.1063/1.4819786 |issn=0021-9606 |pmid=24160524 |doi-access=free |hdl-access=free |hdl=10044/1/12859}}</ref> the simplicity of the Lennard-Jones potential, as well as its often surprising ability to accurately capture real fluid behavior, has historically made it the [[Pair potential|pair-potential]] of greatest general importance.<ref name="Stephan-2020a" />

== History ==
In 1903, [[Gustav Mie]] worked on effective field theories and while Mie's work did not clearly define the potential used, 
later work defined the [[Mie potential]] as a combination of a repulsive potential, <math>1/r^{n}</math>, with an attractive potential, <math>-1/r^{m}</math>, using empirically determined coefficients <math>A_n</math> and <math>B_m</math>:<ref name="FischerWendland"/>
<math display="block"> V(r) = \frac{A_n}{r^{n}} - \frac{B_m}{r^m}.</math>
[[Eduard Grüneisen]] built on Mie work for solids, showing that <math>n>m</math> and <math>m>3</math> is required for solids. As a result of this work the Lennard-Jones potential is sometimes called the Mie−
Grüneisen potential in [[solid-state physics]].<ref name="SchwerdtfegerWales"/>

In 1924, the year that Lennard-Jones received his PhD from [[Cambridge University]], he published<ref name="Jones-1924">{{cite journal |date=1924 |title=On the determination of molecular fields.—I. From the variation of the viscosity of a gas with temperature |journal=Proceedings of the Royal Society of London. Series A, Containing Papers of a Mathematical and Physical Character |language=en |volume=106 |issue=738 |pages=441–462 |doi=10.1098/rspa.1924.0081 |bibcode=1924RSPSA.106..441J |issn=0950-1207 |last1=Jones |first1=J. E. |doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |date=1924 |title=On the determination of molecular fields. —II. From the equation of state of a gas |journal=Proceedings of the Royal Society of London. Series A, Containing Papers of a Mathematical and Physical Character |language=en |volume=106 |issue=738 |pages=463–477 |doi=10.1098/rspa.1924.0082 |bibcode=1924RSPSA.106..463J |issn=0950-1207 |last1=Jones |first1=J. E. |doi-access=free}}</ref> a series of landmark papers on the pair potentials that would ultimately be named for him.<ref name="Lenhard-2024" /><ref name="SchwerdtfegerWales"/><ref name="Lennard-Jonesium" /><ref name="FischerWendland" /> In these papers he adjusted the parameters of the potential then using the result in a model of gas viscosity, seeking a set of values consistent with experiment. His initial results suggested a repulsive <math>n=13.5</math> and an attractive <math>m=3</math>.

In 1930, after the discovery of [[quantum mechanics]], [[Fritz London]] showed that theory predicts the long-range attractive force should have <math>m=6</math>. In his 1931 review,<ref name=LJ_1931>{{cite journal |last=Lennard-Jones |first=J E |date=1931-09-01 |title=Cohesion |url=https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/0959-5309/43/5/301 |journal=Proceedings of the Physical Society |volume=43 |issue=5 |pages=461–482 |doi=10.1088/0959-5309/43/5/301 |bibcode=1931PPS....43..461L |issn=0959-5309|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Lennard-Jones used similar reasoning to suggested using
<math>m=6</math> and <math>n=12</math> based on experimental data.<ref name="FischerWendland">{{Cite journal |last1=Fischer |first1=Johann |last2=Wendland |first2=Martin |date=2023-10-01 |title=On the history of key empirical intermolecular potentials |journal=Fluid Phase Equilibria |volume=573 |article-number=113876 |doi=10.1016/j.fluid.2023.113876 |issn=0378-3812|doi-access=free |bibcode=2023FlPEq.57313876F }}</ref> Setting <math>A_n = 4\varepsilon \sigma^{12}</math> and <math>B_m = 4\varepsilon \sigma^6</math> 
Lennard-Jones applied this form of the potential to describe many properties of fluids setting the stage for many subsequent studies.<ref name="FischerWendland"/>

== Dimensionless (reduced units) ==
{| class="wikitable" style="float:right"
|+dimensionless (reduced) units
|-
! Property !! Symbol !! Reduced form
|-
| Length ||<math>r^{*}</math>||<math>\frac{r}{\sigma}</math>
|-
| Time ||<math>t^{*}</math>||<math>t\sqrt{\frac{\varepsilon}{m\sigma^2}}</math>
|-
| Temperature ||<math>T^{*}</math>||<math>\frac{k_B T}{\varepsilon}</math>
|-
| Force ||<math>F^{*}</math>||<math>\frac{F\sigma}{\varepsilon}</math>
|-
| Energy ||<math>U^{*}</math>||<math>\frac{U}{\varepsilon}</math>
|-
| Pressure ||<math>p^{*}</math>||<math>\frac{p\sigma^3}{\varepsilon}</math>
|-
| Density ||<math>\rho^{*}</math>||<math>\rho\sigma^3</math>
|-
| Surface tension ||<math>\gamma^{*}</math>||<math>\frac{\gamma\sigma^2}{\varepsilon}</math>
|}
Dimensionless reduced units can be defined based on the Lennard-Jones potential parameters, which is convenient for molecular simulations. From a numerical point of view, the advantages of this unit system include computing values which are closer to unity, using simplified equations and being able to easily scale the results.<ref name="Allen-2017">{{cite journal |last1=Allen |first1=Michael P. |last2=Tildesley |first2=Dominic J. |date=2017-11-23 |title=Computer Simulation of Liquids |journal=Oxford Scholarship Online |doi=10.1093/oso/9780198803195.001.0001 |isbn=978-0-19-880319-5}}</ref><ref name="Rapaport2004"/> This reduced units system requires the specification of the size parameter <math>\sigma</math> and the energy parameter <math>\varepsilon</math> of the Lennard-Jones potential and the mass of the particle <math>m</math>. All physical properties can be converted straightforwardly taking the respective dimension into account, see table. The reduced units are often abbreviated and indicated by an asterisk.

In general, reduced units can also be built up on other molecular interaction potentials that consist of a length parameter and an energy parameter.

== Long-range interactions ==
[[File:ExpemplaricObservable.png|class=skin-invert-image|thumb|318x318px|Illustrative example of the convergence of a correction scheme to account for the long-range interactions of the Lennard-Jones potential. Therein, <math>X</math> indicates an exemplaric observable and <math>r_\mathrm{c}</math> the applied cut-off radius. The long-range corrected value is indicated as <math>X_\mathrm{corr}</math> (symbols and line as a guide for the eye); the hypothetical 'true' value as <math>X_\mathrm{true}</math> (dashed line).]]
The Lennard-Jones potential, cf. Eq. (1) and Figure on the top, has an infinite range. Only under its consideration, the 'true' and 'full' Lennard-Jones potential is examined. For the evaluation of an [[observable]] of an ensemble of particles interacting by the Lennard-Jones potential using molecular simulations, the interactions can only be evaluated explicitly up to a certain distance – simply due to the fact that the number of particles will always be finite. The maximum distance applied in a simulation is usually referred to as 'cut-off' radius <math>r_\mathrm{c}</math> (because the Lennard-Jones potential is radially symmetric). To obtain thermophysical properties (both macroscopic or microscopic) of the 'true' and 'full' Lennard-Jones (LJ) potential, the contribution of the potential beyond the cut-off radius has to be accounted for.

Different correction schemes have been developed to account for the influence of the long-range interactions in simulations and to sustain a sufficiently good approximation of the 'full' potential.<ref name="Frenkel-2002"/><ref name="Allen-2017"/> They are based on simplifying assumptions regarding the structure of the fluid. For simple cases, such as in studies of the equilibrium of homogeneous fluids, simple correction terms yield excellent results. In other cases, such as in studies of inhomogeneous systems with different phases, accounting for the long-range interactions is more tedious. These corrections are usually referred to as 'long-range corrections'. For most properties, simple analytical expressions are known and well established. For a given observable <math>X</math>, the 'corrected' simulation result <math>X_\mathrm{corr}</math> is then simply computed from the actually sampled value <math>X_\mathrm{sampled}</math> and the long-range correction value <math>X_\mathrm{lrc}</math>, e.g. for the [[internal energy]] <math>U_\mathrm{corr} = U_\mathrm{sampled} + U_\mathrm{lrc}</math>.<ref name="Allen-2017"/> The hypothetical true value of the observable of the Lennard-Jones potential at truly infinite cut-off distance ([[thermodynamic limit]]) <math>X_\mathrm{true}</math> can in general only be estimated.

Furthermore, the quality of the long-range correction scheme depends on the cut-off radius. The assumptions made with the correction schemes are usually not justified at (very) short cut-off radii. This is illustrated in the example shown in Figure on the right. The long-range correction scheme is said to be converged, if the remaining error of the correction scheme is sufficiently small at a given cut-off distance, cf. Figure.

== Extensions and modifications ==
The Lennard-Jones potential – as an archetype for [[interatomic potential|intermolecular potentials]] – has been used numerous times as starting point for the development of more elaborate or more generalized intermolecular potentials. Various extensions and modifications of the Lennard-Jones potential have been proposed in the literature; a more extensive list is given in the '[[interatomic potential]]' article. The following list refers only to several example potentials that are directly related to the Lennard-Jones potential and are of both historic importance and still relevant for present research.

* '''[[Mie potential]]''' The Mie potential is the generalized version of the Lennard-Jones potential, i.e. the exponents 12 and 6 are introduced as parameters <math>\lambda_\mathrm{rep}</math> and <math>\lambda_\mathrm{attr}</math>. Especially thermodynamic derivative properties, e.g. the [[compressibility]] and the [[speed of sound]], are known to be very sensitive to the steepness of the repulsive part of the intermolecular potential, which can therefore be modeled more sophisticated by the Mie potential.<ref name="Lafitte-2013"/> The first explicit formulation of the Mie potential is attributed to [[Eduard Grüneisen]].<ref>{{cite journal |last=Grüneisen |first=Edward |year=1911 |title=Das Verhältnis der thermischen Ausdehnung zur spezifischen Wärme fester Elemente |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1002/bbpc.191100004 |journal=Zeitschrift für Elektrochemie und angewandte physikalische Chemie |volume=17 |issue=17 |pages=737–739 |doi=10.1002/bbpc.191100004 |s2cid=178760389 |url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last=Grüneisen |first=E. |date=1912 |title=Theorie des festen Zustandes einatomiger Elemente |journal=Annalen der Physik |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1002/andp.19123441202 |language=de |volume=344 |issue=12 |pages=257–306 |doi=10.1002/andp.19123441202 |bibcode=1912AnP...344..257G}}</ref> Hence, the Mie potential was actually proposed before the Lennard-Jones potential. The Mie potential is named after [[Gustav Mie]].<ref name="Mie-1903"/>
* '''[[Buckingham potential]]''' The Buckingham potential was proposed by [[Richard Buckingham]]. The repulsive part of the Lennard-Jones potential is therein replaced by an exponential function and it incorporates an additional parameter.
* '''[[Stockmayer potential]]''' The Stockmayer potential is named after W.H. Stockmayer.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Stockmayer |first=W. H. |date=1941-05-01 |title=Second Virial Coefficients of Polar Gases |url=https://aip.scitation.org/doi/10.1063/1.1750922 |journal=The Journal of Chemical Physics |volume=9 |issue=5 |pages=398–402 |doi=10.1063/1.1750922 |bibcode=1941JChPh...9..398S |issn=0021-9606|url-access=subscription }}</ref> The Stockmayer potential is a combination of a Lennard-Jones potential superimposed by a dipole. Hence, Stockmayer particles are not spherically symmetric, but rather have an important orientational structure.
* '''Two center Lennard-Jones potential''' The two center Lennard-Jones potential consists of two identical Lennard-Jones interaction sites (same <math>\varepsilon</math>, <math>\sigma</math>, <math>m</math>) that are bonded as a rigid body. It is often abbreviated as 2CLJ. Usually, the elongation (distance between the Lennard-Jones sites) is significantly smaller than the size parameter <math>\sigma</math>. Hence, the two interaction sites are significantly fused.
* '''Lennard-Jones truncated & splined potential''' The Lennard-Jones truncated & splined potential is a rarely used yet useful potential. Similar to the more popular LJTS potential, it is sturdily truncated at a certain 'end' distance <math>r_\mathrm{end}</math> and no long-range interactions are considered beyond. While the LJTS potential is shifted such that the potential is continuous but the force is discontinuous, the Lennard-Jones truncated & splined potential is made continuous by using a spline function that ensures a continuous force.

=== Lennard-Jones truncated & shifted (LJTS) potential ===
[[File:Vapor liquid equilibrium properties of LJ and LJTS potential.png|class=skin-invert-image|thumb|770x770px|Comparison of the vapor–liquid equilibrium of the 'full' Lennard-Jones potential (black) and the 'Lennard-Jones truncated & shifted' potential (blue). The symbols indicate molecular simulation results;<ref name="Stephan-2019b"/><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Vrabec |first1=Jadran |last2=Kedia |first2=Gaurav Kumar |last3=Fuchs |first3=Guido |last4=Hasse |first4=Hans |date=2006-05-10 |title=Comprehensive study of the vapour–liquid coexistence of the truncated and shifted Lennard–Jones fluid including planar and spherical interface properties |url=https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/00268970600556774 |journal=Molecular Physics |language=en |volume=104 |issue=9 |pages=1509–1527 |doi=10.1080/00268970600556774 |bibcode=2006MolPh.104.1509V |s2cid=96606562 |issn=0026-8976|url-access=subscription }}</ref> the lines indicate results from equations of state.<ref name="Stephan-2020a"/><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Heier |first1=Michaela |last2=Stephan |first2=Simon |last3=Liu |first3=Jinlu |last4=Chapman |first4=Walter G. |last5=Hasse |first5=Hans |last6=Langenbach |first6=Kai |date=2018-08-18 |title=Equation of state for the Lennard-Jones truncated and shifted fluid with a cut-off radius of 2.5 σ based on perturbation theory and its applications to interfacial thermodynamics |url=https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/00268976.2018.1447153 |journal=Molecular Physics |language=en |volume=116 |issue=15–16 |pages=2083–2094 |doi=10.1080/00268976.2018.1447153 |bibcode=2018MolPh.116.2083H |s2cid=102956189 |issn=0026-8976}}</ref>]]
The Lennard-Jones truncated & shifted (LJTS) potential is an often used alternative to the 'full' Lennard-Jones potential (see Eq. (1)). The 'full' and the 'truncated & shifted' Lennard-Jones potential have to be kept strictly separate. They are simply two different intermolecular potentials yielding different thermophysical properties. The Lennard-Jones truncated & shifted potential is defined as
<math display="block">
 V_{\text{LJTS}}(r) = \begin{cases}
   V_\text{LJ} (r)
   -
   V_\text{LJ} (r_\text{end})
   &
   ~~~~ r \le r_\text{end}
   \\
   0
   &
   ~~~~ r > r_\text{end},
\end{cases}</math>
with
<math display="block">
V_\text{LJ}(r)
=
4 \varepsilon
\left[
   \left( \frac{\sigma}{r} \right)^{12}
   -
   \left( \frac{\sigma}{r} \right)^6
\right].
</math>

Hence, the LJTS potential is truncated at <math> r_\mathrm{end} </math> and shifted by the corresponding energy value <math> V_\mathrm{LJ}(r_\mathrm{end})</math>. The latter is applied to avoid a discontinuity jump of the potential at <math> r_\mathrm{end} </math>. For the LJTS potential, no long-range interactions beyond <math> r_\mathrm{end} </math> are required – neither explicitly nor implicitly. The most frequently used version of the Lennard-Jones truncated & shifted potential is the one with <math> r_\mathrm{end} = 2.5\,\sigma </math>.{{citation needed|date=May 2024}} Nevertheless, different <math> r_\mathrm{end} </math> values have been used in the literature.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Shaul |first1=Katherine R. S. |last2=Schultz |first2=Andrew J. |last3=Kofke |first3=David A. |date=2010 |title=The effect of truncation and shift on virial coefficients of Lennard–Jones potentials |url=http://cccc.uochb.cas.cz/75/4/0447/ |journal=Collection of Czechoslovak Chemical Communications |language=en |volume=75 |issue=4 |pages=447–462 |doi=10.1135/cccc2009113 |issn=1212-6950|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Shi |first1=Wei |last2=Johnson |first2=J.Karl |date=2001 |title=Histogram reweighting and finite-size scaling study of the Lennard–Jones fluids |journal=Fluid Phase Equilibria |language=en |volume=187-188 |pages=171–191 |doi=10.1016/S0378-3812(01)00534-9|bibcode=2001FlPEq.187..171S }}</ref><ref name="Dunikov-2001">{{cite journal |last1=Dunikov |first1=D. O. |last2=Malyshenko |first2=S. P. |last3=Zhakhovskii |first3=V. V. |date=2001-10-08 |title=Corresponding states law and molecular dynamics simulations of the Lennard-Jones fluid |url=https://aip.scitation.org/doi/10.1063/1.1396674 |journal=The Journal of Chemical Physics |language=en |volume=115 |issue=14 |pages=6623–6631 |doi=10.1063/1.1396674 |bibcode=2001JChPh.115.6623D |issn=0021-9606|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>[https://pubs.rsc.org/en/content/articlelanding/2017/CP/C7CP02923C Lívia B. Pártay, Christoph Ortner, Albert P. Bartók, Chris J. Pickard, and Gábor Csányi "Polytypism in the ground state structure of the Lennard-Jonesium", Physical Chemistry Chemical Physics '''19''' 19369 (2017)]</ref> Each LJTS potential with a given truncation radius <math> r_\mathrm{end} </math> has to be considered as a potential and accordingly a substance of its own.

The LJTS potential is computationally significantly cheaper than the 'full' Lennard-Jones potential, but still covers the essential physical features of matter (the presence of a critical and a triple point, soft repulsive and attractive interactions, phase equilibria etc.). Therefore, the LJTS potential is used for the testing of new algorithms, simulation methods, and new physical theories.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Tchipev |first1=Nikola |last2=Seckler |first2=Steffen |last3=Heinen |first3=Matthias |last4=Vrabec |first4=Jadran |last5=Gratl |first5=Fabio |last6=Horsch |first6=Martin |last7=Bernreuther |first7=Martin |last8=Glass |first8=Colin W |last9=Niethammer |first9=Christoph |last10=Hammer |first10=Nicolay |last11=Krischok |first11=Bernd |date=2019 |title=TweTriS: Twenty trillion-atom simulation |url=https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/1094342018819741 |journal=The International Journal of High Performance Computing Applications |language=en |volume=33 |issue=5 |pages=838–854 |doi=10.1177/1094342018819741 |s2cid=59345875 |issn=1094-3420|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Stephan |first1=Simon |last2=Liu |first2=Jinlu |last3=Langenbach |first3=Kai |last4=Chapman |first4=Walter G. |last5=Hasse |first5=Hans |date=2018 |title=Vapor−Liquid Interface of the Lennard-Jones Truncated and Shifted Fluid: Comparison of Molecular Simulation, Density Gradient Theory, and Density Functional Theory |url=https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/acs.jpcc.8b06332 |journal=The Journal of Physical Chemistry C |language=en |volume=122 |issue=43 |pages=24705–24715 |doi=10.1021/acs.jpcc.8b06332 |s2cid=105759822 |issn=1932-7447|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Kob |first1=Walter |last2=Andersen |first2=Hans C. |date=1995-05-01 |title=Testing mode-coupling theory for a supercooled binary Lennard-Jones mixture I: The van Hove correlation function |url=https://journals.aps.org/pre/abstract/10.1103/PhysRevE.51.4626 |journal=Physical Review E |volume=51 |issue=5 |pages=4626–4641 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevE.51.4626 |pmid=9963176 |arxiv=cond-mat/9501102 |bibcode=1995PhRvE..51.4626K |s2cid=17662741}}</ref>

Interestingly, for homogeneous systems, the intermolecular forces that are calculated from the LJ and the LJTS potential at a given distance are the same (since <math> \text{d}V/\text{d}r </math> is the same), whereas the potential energy and the pressure are affected by the shifting. Also, the properties of the LJTS substance may furthermore be affected by the chosen simulation algorithm, i.e. MD or MC sampling (this is in general not the case for the 'full' Lennard-Jones potential).

For the LJTS potential with <math> r_\mathrm{end} = 2.5\,\sigma </math>, the potential energy shift is approximately 1/60 of the dispersion energy at the potential well: <math> V_\mathrm{LJ}(r_\mathrm{end} = 2.5\,\sigma) = -0.0163\,\varepsilon </math>. The Figure on the right shows the comparison of the [[vapor–liquid equilibrium]] of the 'full' Lennard-Jones potential and the 'Lennard-Jones truncated & shifted' potential. The 'full' Lennard-Jones potential results prevail a significantly higher [[critical point (thermodynamics)|critical temperature]] and pressure compared to the LJTS potential results, but the critical density is very similar.<ref name="Stephan e1699185"/><ref name="Smit-1992"/><ref name="Dunikov-2001"/> The [[vapor pressure]] and the [[enthalpy of vaporization]] are influenced more strongly by the long-range interactions than the saturated densities. This is due to the fact that the potential is manipulated mainly energetically by the truncation and shifting.

== Applications ==
The Lennard-Jones potential is not only of fundamental importance in [[computational chemistry]] and [[soft matter|soft-matter physics]], but also for the modeling of real substances. The Lennard-Jones potential is used for fundamental studies on the behavior of matter and for elucidating atomistic phenomena. It is also often used for somewhat special use cases, e.g. for studying thermophysical properties of two- or four-dimensional substances<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Smit |first1=B. |last2=Frenkel |first2=D. |date=1991-04-15 |title=Vapor–liquid equilibria of the two-dimensional Lennard-Jones fluid(s) |url=https://aip.scitation.org/doi/10.1063/1.460477 |journal=The Journal of Chemical Physics |volume=94 |issue=8 |pages=5663–5668 |doi=10.1063/1.460477 |bibcode=1991JChPh..94.5663S |s2cid=1580499 |issn=0021-9606}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last=Scalise |first=Osvaldo H |date=June 2001 |title=Type I gas–liquid equilibria of a two-dimensional Lennard–Jones binary mixture |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0378381201003806 |journal=Fluid Phase Equilibria |volume=182 |issue=1–2 |pages=59–64 |doi=10.1016/s0378-3812(01)00380-6 |bibcode=2001FlPEq.182...59S |issn=0378-3812|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Hloucha |first1=M. |last2=Sandler |first2=S. I. |date=November 1999 |title=Phase diagram of the four-dimensional Lennard-Jones fluid |url=https://aip.scitation.org/doi/10.1063/1.480138 |journal=The Journal of Chemical Physics |volume=111 |issue=17 |pages=8043–8047 |doi=10.1063/1.480138 |bibcode=1999JChPh.111.8043H |issn=0021-9606|url-access=subscription }}</ref> (instead of the classical three spatial directions of our universe).

There are two main applications of the Lennard-Jones potentials: (i) for studying the hypothetical Lennard-Jones substance<ref name="Lennard-Jonesium" /> and (ii) for modeling interactions in real substance models.<ref name="SchwerdtfegerWales" /><ref name="Lenhard-2024" /> These two applications are discussed in the following.

=== Lennard-Jones substance ===
A Lennard-Jones substance or "Lennard-Jonesium" is the name given to an idealized substance which would result from atoms or molecules interacting exclusively through the Lennard-Jones potential.<ref name="Lennard-Jonesium">{{Cite journal |last1=Lenhard |first1=Johannes |last2=Stephan |first2=Simon |last3=Hasse |first3=Hans |date=February 2024 |title=A child of prediction. On the History, Ontology, and Computation of the Lennard-Jonesium |url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S0039368123001668 |journal=Studies in History and Philosophy of Science |language=en |volume=103 |pages=105–113 |doi=10.1016/j.shpsa.2023.11.007|pmid=38128443 |s2cid=266440296 |url-access=subscription }}</ref> 
[[Statistical mechanics]]<ref name="Hill, Terrell L.-1956"/> and [[molecular dynamics|computer simulations]]<ref name="Rapaport2004">{{cite book |author=D. C. Rapaport |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=iqDJ2hjqBMEC |title=The Art of Molecular Dynamics Simulation |date=1 April 2004 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |isbn=978-0-521-82568-9}}</ref><ref name="Frenkel-2002">{{citation |last1=Frenkel |first1=D. |last2=Smit |first2=B. |title=Understanding Molecular Simulation |year=2002 |edition=Second |location=San Diego |publisher=Academic Press |isbn=0-12-267351-4}}</ref> can be used to study the Lennard-Jones potential and to obtain thermophysical properties of the 'Lennard-Jones substance'. The Lennard-Jones substance is often referred to as 'Lennard-Jonesium,'<ref name="Lennard-Jonesium"/> suggesting that it is viewed as a (fictive) [[chemical element]].<ref name="Stephan-2019b" />  Moreover, its energy and length parameters can be adjusted to fit many different real substances. Both the Lennard-Jones potential and, accordingly, the Lennard-Jones substance are simplified yet realistic models, such as they accurately capture essential physical principles like the presence of a [[critical point (thermodynamics)|critical]] and a [[triple point]], [[condensation]] and [[freezing]]. Due in part to its mathematical simplicity, the Lennard-Jones potential has been extensively used in studies on matter since the early days of computer simulation.<ref name="Wood-1957"/><ref name="Rosenbluth-1954"/><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Alder |first1=B. J. |last2=Wainwright |first2=T. E. |date=1959 |title=Studies in Molecular Dynamics. I. General Method |url=https://aip.scitation.org/doi/10.1063/1.1730376 |journal=The Journal of Chemical Physics |language=en |volume=31 |issue=2 |pages=459–466 |doi=10.1063/1.1730376 |bibcode=1959JChPh..31..459A |issn=0021-9606|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last=Rahman |first=A. |date=1964-10-19 |title=Correlations in the Motion of Atoms in Liquid Argon |url=https://link.aps.org/doi/10.1103/PhysRev.136.A405 |journal=Physical Review |language=en |volume=136 |issue=2A |pages=A405–A411 |doi=10.1103/PhysRev.136.A405 |bibcode=1964PhRv..136..405R |issn=0031-899X|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

==== Thermophysical properties of the Lennard-Jones substance ====
[[File:LJ PhaseDiagram.png|class=skin-invert-image|thumb|347x347px|Phase diagram of the Lennard-Jones substance. Correlations and numeric values for the critical point and triple point(s) are taken from Refs.<ref name="Stephan-2019b"/><ref name="Schultz-2018"/><ref name="Stephan-2020a"/> The star indicates the critical point.<ref name="Stephan-2019b"/> The circle indicates the vapor–liquid–solid triple point and the triangle indicates the vapor–solid (fcc)–solid (hcp) triple point.<ref name="Schultz-2018"/><ref name="Schultz-2020">{{cite journal |last1=Schultz |first1=Andrew J. |last2=Kofke |first2=David A. |date=2020-08-07 |title=Erratum: "Comprehensive high-precision high-accuracy equation of state and coexistence properties for classical Lennard-Jones crystals and low-temperature fluid phases" [J. Chem. Phys. 149, 204508 (2018)] |journal=The Journal of Chemical Physics |language=en |volume=153 |issue=5 |page=059901 |doi=10.1063/5.0021283 |pmid=32770918 |issn=0021-9606 |doi-access=free|bibcode=2020JChPh.153e9901S }}</ref> The solid lines indicate coexistence lines of two phases.<ref name="Stephan-2019b">{{cite journal |last1=Stephan |first1=Simon |last2=Thol |first2=Monika |last3=Vrabec |first3=Jadran |last4=Hasse |first4=Hans |date=2019-10-28 |title=Thermophysical Properties of the Lennard-Jones Fluid: Database and Data Assessment |url=https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/acs.jcim.9b00620 |journal=Journal of Chemical Information and Modeling |language=en |volume=59 |issue=10 |pages=4248–4265 |doi=10.1021/acs.jcim.9b00620 |pmid=31609113 |s2cid=204545481 |issn=1549-9596|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref name="Schultz-2018">{{cite journal |last1=Schultz |first1=Andrew J. |last2=Kofke |first2=David A. |date=2018-11-28 |title=Comprehensive high-precision high-accuracy equation of state and coexistence properties for classical Lennard-Jones crystals and low-temperature fluid phases |url=https://aip.scitation.org/doi/10.1063/1.5053714 |journal=The Journal of Chemical Physics |volume=149 |issue=20 |page=204508 |doi=10.1063/1.5053714 |pmid=30501268 |bibcode=2018JChPh.149t4508S |s2cid=54629914 |issn=0021-9606|url-access=subscription }}</ref> The dashed lines indicate the vapor–liquid spinodal.<ref name="Stephan-2020a"/> ]]
Thermophysical properties of the Lennard-Jones substance,<ref name="Lennard-Jonesium"/> i.e. particles interacting with the Lennard-Jones potential can be obtained using statistical mechanics. Some properties can be computed analytically, i.e. with machine precision, whereas most properties can only be obtained by performing molecular simulations.<ref name="Rapaport2004"/> The latter will in general be superimposed by both statistical and systematic uncertainties.<ref name="Schappals-2017">{{cite journal |last1=Schappals |first1=Michael |last2=Mecklenfeld |first2=Andreas |last3=Kröger |first3=Leif |last4=Botan |first4=Vitalie |last5=Köster |first5=Andreas |last6=Stephan |first6=Simon |last7=García |first7=Edder J. |last8=Rutkai |first8=Gabor |last9=Raabe |first9=Gabriele |last10=Klein |first10=Peter |last11=Leonhard |first11=Kai |date=2017-09-12 |title=Round Robin Study: Molecular Simulation of Thermodynamic Properties from Models with Internal Degrees of Freedom |url=https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/acs.jctc.7b00489 |journal=Journal of Chemical Theory and Computation |language=en |volume=13 |issue=9 |pages=4270–4280 |doi=10.1021/acs.jctc.7b00489 |pmid=28738147 |issn=1549-9618|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref name="Stephan-2019b"/><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Loeffler |first1=Hannes H. |last2=Bosisio |first2=Stefano |last3=Duarte Ramos Matos |first3=Guilherme |last4=Suh |first4=Donghyuk |last5=Roux |first5=Benoit |last6=Mobley |first6=David L. |last7=Michel |first7=Julien |date=2018-11-13 |title=Reproducibility of Free Energy Calculations across Different Molecular Simulation Software Packages |url=https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/acs.jctc.8b00544 |journal=Journal of Chemical Theory and Computation |language=en |volume=14 |issue=11 |pages=5567–5582 |doi=10.1021/acs.jctc.8b00544 |pmid=30289712 |hdl=20.500.11820/52d85d71-d3df-468b-8f88-9c52e83da1f1 |s2cid=52923832 |issn=1549-9618|hdl-access=free }}</ref><ref name="Lenhard-2019">{{cite journal |last1=Lenhard |first1=Johannes |last2=Küster |first2=Uwe |date=2019 |title=Reproducibility and the Concept of Numerical Solution |url=https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11023-019-09492-9 |journal=Minds and Machines |language=en |volume=29 |issue=1 |pages=19–36 |doi=10.1007/s11023-019-09492-9 |s2cid=59159685 |issn=0924-6495|url-access=subscription }}</ref> The virial coefficients can for example be computed directly from the Lennard-potential using algebraic expressions<ref name="Hill, Terrell L.-1956">{{cite book |last=Hill, Terrell L. |title=Statistical mechanics: principles and selected applications |date=1956 |publisher=Dover Publications |isbn=0-486-65390-0 |location=New York |oclc=15163657}}</ref> and reported data has therefore no uncertainty. Molecular simulation results, e.g. the pressure at a given temperature and density has both statistical and systematic uncertainties.<ref name="Schappals-2017"/><ref name="Lenhard-2019"/> Molecular simulations of the Lennard-Jones potential can in general be performed using either [[molecular dynamics]] (MD) simulations or [[Monte Carlo method|Monte Carlo]] (MC) simulation. For MC simulations, the Lennard-Jones potential <math>V_\mathrm{LJ}(r)</math> is directly used, whereas MD simulations are always based on the derivative of the potential, i.e. the force <math>F = -\mathrm{d}V / \mathrm{d}r</math>. These differences in combination with differences in the treatment of the long-range interactions (see below) can influence computed thermophysical properties.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Shi |first1=Wei |last2=Johnson |first2=J. Karl |date=2001-09-15 |title=Histogram reweighting and finite-size scaling study of the Lennard–Jones fluids |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0378381201005349 |journal=Fluid Phase Equilibria |language=en |volume=187-188 |pages=171–191 |doi=10.1016/S0378-3812(01)00534-9 |bibcode=2001FlPEq.187..171S |issn=0378-3812|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref name="Smit-1992">{{citation |last=Smit |first=B. |title=Phase diagrams of Lennard-Jones fluids |url=https://pure.uva.nl/ws/files/2199981/29999_3595309057smi922.pdf |journal=[[Journal of Chemical Physics]] |volume=96 |issue=11 |pages=8639–8640 |year=1992 |bibcode=1992JChPh..96.8639S |doi=10.1063/1.462271}}</ref>

Since the ''Lennard-Jonesium'' is the archetype for the modeling of simple yet realistic intermolecular interactions, a large number of thermophysical properties were studied and reported in the literature.<ref name="Stephan-2019b"/> Computer experiment data of the Lennard-Jones potential is presently considered the most accurately known data in classical mechanics computational chemistry. Hence, such data is also mostly used as a benchmark for validating and testing new algorithms and theories. The Lennard-Jones potential has been constantly used since the early days of molecular simulations. The first results from computer experiments for the Lennard-Jones potential were reported by Rosenbluth and Rosenbluth<ref name="Rosenbluth-1954">{{cite journal |last1=Rosenbluth |first1=Marshall N. |last2=Rosenbluth |first2=Arianna W. |date=1954 |title=Further Results on Monte Carlo Equations of State |url=https://aip.scitation.org/doi/10.1063/1.1740207 |journal=The Journal of Chemical Physics |language=en |volume=22 |issue=5 |pages=881–884 |doi=10.1063/1.1740207 |bibcode=1954JChPh..22..881R |issn=0021-9606|url-access=subscription }}</ref> and Wood and Parker<ref name="Wood-1957">{{cite journal |last1=Wood |first1=W. W. |last2=Parker |first2=F. R. |date=1957 |title=Monte Carlo Equation of State of Molecules Interacting with the Lennard-Jones Potential. I. A Supercritical Isotherm at about Twice the Critical Temperature |url=https://aip.scitation.org/doi/10.1063/1.1743822 |journal=The Journal of Chemical Physics |language=en |volume=27 |issue=3 |pages=720–733 |doi=10.1063/1.1743822 |bibcode=1957JChPh..27..720W |issn=0021-9606|url-access=subscription }}</ref> after molecular simulations on "[[Equation of State Calculations by Fast Computing Machines|fast computing machines]]" became available in 1953.<ref name="Metropolis-1953"/> Since then many studies reported data of the Lennard-Jones substance;<ref name="Stephan-2019b"/> approximately 50,000 data points are publicly available. The current state of research on the thermophysical properties of the Lennard-Jones substance is summarized by Stephan et al.<ref name="Stephan-2019b"/> (which did not cover transport and mixture properties). The US [[National Institute of Standards and Technology]] (NIST)  provides examples of molecular dynamics and Monte Carlo codes along with results obtained from them.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Daniel Siderius |url=https://data.nist.gov/od/id/FF429BC178798B3EE0431A570681E858232 |title=NIST Standard Reference Simulation Website - SRD 173 |date=2017-09-01 |publisher=National Institute of Standards and Technology |language=en |doi=10.18434/T4M88Q}}</ref> Transport property data of Lennard-Jones fluids have been compiled by Bell et al.<ref>{{Cite journal |title=Modified Entropy Scaling of the Transport Properties of the Lennard-Jones Fluid |url=http://dx.doi.org/10.1021/acs.jpcb.9b05808.s001 |access-date=2024-05-20 |doi=10.1021/acs.jpcb.9b05808 | journal = The Journal of Physical Chemistry B|date=2019 |pmc=7147083 |last1=Bell |first1=Ian H. |last2=Messerly |first2=Richard |last3=Thol |first3=Monika |last4=Costigliola |first4=Lorenzo |last5=Dyre |first5=Jeppe C. |volume=123 |issue=29 |pages=6345–6363 |pmid=31241958 }}</ref> and Lautenschaeger and Hasse.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Lautenschläger |first1=Martin P. |last2=Hasse |first2=Hans |date=2021-04-29 |title=Transport Properties of the Lennard-Jones Truncated and Shifted Fluid from Non-equilibrium Molecular Dynamics Simulations |doi=10.31219/osf.io/67w4u }}</ref>

Figure on the right shows the [[phase diagram]] of the Lennard-Jones fluid. Phase equilibria of the Lennard-Jones potential have been studied numerous times and are accordingly known today with good precision.<ref name="Schultz-2018"/><ref name="Stephan-2019b"/><ref name="Köster-2017">{{cite journal |last1=Köster |first1=Andreas |last2=Mausbach |first2=Peter |last3=Vrabec |first3=Jadran |date=2017-10-10 |title=Premelting, solid–fluid equilibria, and thermodynamic properties in the high density region based on the Lennard-Jones potential |url=https://aip.scitation.org/doi/10.1063/1.4990667 |journal=The Journal of Chemical Physics |volume=147 |issue=14 |page=144502 |doi=10.1063/1.4990667 |pmid=29031254 |bibcode=2017JChPh.147n4502K |issn=0021-9606|url-access=subscription }}</ref> The Figure shows results correlations derived from computer experiment results (hence, lines instead of data points are shown).

The mean intermolecular interaction of a Lennard-Jones particle strongly depends on the [[thermodynamic state]], i.e., temperature and pressure (or density). For solid states, the attractive Lennard-Jones interaction plays a dominant role – especially at low temperatures. For liquid states, no ordered structure is present compared to solid states. The mean potential energy per particle is negative. For gaseous states, attractive interactions of the Lennard-Jones potential play a minor role – since they are far distanced. The main part of the internal energy is stored as [[kinetic energy]] for gaseous states. At supercritical states, the attractive Lennard-Jones interaction plays a minor role. With increasing temperature, the mean kinetic energy of the particles increases and exceeds the energy well of the Lennard-Jones potential. Hence, the particles mainly interact by the potentials' soft repulsive interactions and the mean potential energy per particle is accordingly positive.

Overall, due to the large timespan the Lennard-Jones potential has been studied and thermophysical property data has been reported in the literature and computational resources were insufficient for accurate simulations (to modern standards), a noticeable amount of data is known to be dubious.<ref name="Stephan-2019b"/> Nevertheless, in many studies such data is used as reference. The lack of data repositories and data assessment is a crucial element for future work in the long-going field of Lennard-Jones potential research.

===== Characteristic points and curves =====
The most important characteristic points of the Lennard-Jones potential are the [[critical point (thermodynamics)|critical point]] and the vapor–liquid–solid [[triple point]]. They were studied numerous times in the literature and compiled in Ref.<ref name="Stephan-2019b"/> The critical point was thereby assessed to be located at

* <math>T_\mathrm{c} = 1.321 \pm 0.007\,\varepsilon k_\mathrm{B}^{-1}</math>
* <math>\rho_\mathrm{c} = 0.316 \pm 0.005\,\sigma^{-3}</math>
* <math>p_\mathrm{c} = 0.129 \pm 0.005\,\varepsilon\sigma^{-3}</math>

The given uncertainties were calculated from the standard deviation of the critical parameters derived from the most reliable available [[vapor–liquid equilibrium]] data sets.<ref name="Stephan-2019b"/> These uncertainties can be assumed as a lower limit to the accuracy with which the critical point of fluid can be obtained from molecular simulation results.
[[File:CharacteristicCurves.png|class=skin-invert-image|thumb|317x317px|Characteristic curves of the Lennard-Jones substance. The thick black line indicates the vapor–liquid equilibrium; the star indicates the critical point. The brown line indicates the solid–fluid equilibrium. Other black solid lines and symbols indicate Brown's characteristic curves (see text for details) of the Lennard-Jones substance: lines are results from an [[equation of state]], symbols from molecular simulations and triangles exact data in the ideal gas limit obtained from the virial coefficients. Data taken from.<ref name="Stephan-2020b"/><ref name="Deiters 2720–2728">{{cite journal |last1=Deiters |first1=Ulrich K. |last2=Neumaier |first2=Arnold |date=2016-08-11 |title=Computer Simulation of the Characteristic Curves of Pure Fluids |url=https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/acs.jced.6b00133 |journal=Journal of Chemical & Engineering Data |language=en |volume=61 |issue=8 |pages=2720–2728 |doi=10.1021/acs.jced.6b00133 |issn=0021-9568|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref name="Agrawal-1995">{{cite journal |last1=Agrawal |first1=Rupal |last2=Kofke |first2=David A. |date=1995 |title=Thermodynamic and structural properties of model systems at solid–fluid coexistence: II. Melting and sublimation of the Lennard-Jones system |url=https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/00268979500100921 |journal=Molecular Physics |language=en |volume=85 |issue=1 |pages=43–59 |doi=10.1080/00268979500100921 |issn=0026-8976|url-access=subscription }}</ref>|alt=]]
The triple point is presently assumed to be located at

* <math>T_\mathrm{tr} = 0.69 \pm 0.005 \,\varepsilon k_\mathrm{B}^{-1}</math>
* <math>\rho_\mathrm{tr,gas} = 0.0017 \pm 0.004 \,\sigma^{-3}</math>
* <math>\rho_\mathrm{tr,liq} = 0.845 \pm 0.009 \,\sigma^{-3}</math>
* <math>\rho_\mathrm{tr,sol} = 0.961 \pm 0.007 \,\sigma^{-3}</math>
* <math>p_\mathrm{tr} = 0.0012 \pm 0.0007 \,\varepsilon\sigma^{-3}</math>

The uncertainties represent the scattering of data from different authors.<ref name="Schultz-2018"/> The critical point of the Lennard-Jones substance has been studied far more often than the triple point. For both the critical point and the vapor–liquid–solid triple point, several studies reported results out of the above stated ranges. The above stated data is the presently assumed correct and reliable data. Nevertheless, the determinateness of the critical temperature and the triple point temperature is still unsatisfactory.

Evidently, the phase coexistence curves (cf. figures) are of fundamental importance to characterize the Lennard-Jones potential. Furthermore, ''Brown's characteristic curves''<ref>{{cite journal |last=Brown |first=E.H. |year=1960 |title=On the thermodynamic properties of fluids |journal=Bulletin de l'Institut International du Froid |volume=Annexe 1960-1 |pages=169–178}}</ref> yield an illustrative description of essential features of the Lennard-Jones potential. Brown's characteristic curves are defined as curves on which a certain thermodynamic property of the substance matches that of an [[ideal gas]]. For a real fluid, <math>Z</math> and its derivatives can match the values of the ideal gas for special <math>T</math>, <math>\rho</math> combinations only as a result of Gibbs' phase rule. The resulting points collectively constitute a characteristic curve. Four main characteristic curves are defined: One 0th-order (named ''Zeno curve'') and three 1st-order curves (named ''Amagat'', ''Boyle'', and ''Charles curve''). The characteristic curve are required to have a negative or zero curvature throughout and a single maximum in a double-logarithmic pressure-temperature diagram. Furthermore, Brown's characteristic curves and the virial coefficients are directly linked in the limit of the ideal gas and are therefore known exactly at <math>\rho \rightarrow 0</math>. Both computer simulation results and equation of state results have been reported in the literature for the Lennard-Jones potential.<ref name="Deiters 2720–2728"/><ref name="Stephan-2019b"/><ref name="Stephan-2020b"/><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Apfelbaum |first1=E. M. |last2=Vorob'ev |first2=V. S. |date=2020-06-18 |title=The Line of the Unit Compressibility Factor (Zeno-Line) for Crystal States |url=https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/acs.jpcb.0c02749 |journal=The Journal of Physical Chemistry B |language=en |volume=124 |issue=24 |pages=5021–5027 |doi=10.1021/acs.jpcb.0c02749 |pmid=32437611 |s2cid=218835048 |issn=1520-6106|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Apfelbaum |first1=E. M. |last2=Vorob'ev |first2=V. S. |last3=Martynov |first3=G. A. |date=2008 |title=Regarding the Theory of the Zeno Line |url=https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/jp802999z |journal=The Journal of Physical Chemistry A |language=en |volume=112 |issue=26 |pages=6042–6044 |doi=10.1021/jp802999z |pmid=18543889 |bibcode=2008JPCA..112.6042A |issn=1089-5639|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

Points on the Zeno curve Z have a [[compressibility factor]] of unity <math>Z=p/(\rho T)=1</math>. The Zeno curve originates at the [[Boyle temperature]] <math>T_\mathrm{B} = 3.417927982\,\varepsilon k_\mathrm{B}^{-1}</math>, surrounds the critical point, and has a slope of unity in the low temperature limit.<ref name="Stephan-2020b"/> Points on the Boyle curve B have <math>\left.\frac{\mathrm{d}Z}{\mathrm{d}(1/\rho)}\right|_T = 0</math>. The Boyle curve originates with the Zeno curve at the Boyle temperature, faintly surrounds the critical point, and ends on the vapor pressure curve. Points on the Charles curve (a.k.a. [[Joule–Thomson effect|Joule-Thomson inversion curve]]) have <math>\left.\frac{\mathrm{d}Z}{\mathrm{d}T}\right|_p = 0</math> and more importantly <math>\left.\frac{\mathrm{d}T}{\mathrm{d}p}\right|_h = 0</math>, i.e. no temperature change upon isenthalpic throttling. It originates at <math>T= 6.430798418\,\varepsilon k_\mathrm{B}^{-1}</math> in the ideal gas limit, crosses the Zeno curve, and terminates on the vapor pressure curve. Points on the Amagat curve A have <math>\left.\frac{\mathrm{d}Z}{\mathrm{d}T}\right|_\rho = 0</math>. It also starts in the ideal gas limit at <math>T=25.15242837\,\varepsilon k_\mathrm{B}^{-1}</math>, surrounds the critical point and the other three characteristic curves and passes into the solid phase region. A comprehensive discussion of the characteristic curves of the Lennard-Jones potential is given by Stephan and Deiters.<ref name="Stephan-2020b"/>
[[File:VirialCoeff.png|class=skin-invert-image|left|thumb|388x388px|Virial coefficients from the Lennard-Jones potential as a function of the temperature: Second virial coefficient <math>B</math> (top) and third virial coefficient <math>C</math> (bottom). The circle indicates the Boyle temperature <math>T_\mathrm{B}</math>. Results taken from.<ref name="Stephan-2020b"/>]]

===== Properties of the Lennard-Jones fluid =====
[[File:Vapor liquid equilibrium properties of LJ potential.png|class=skin-invert-image|thumb|726x726px|Vapor–liquid equilibrium of the Lennard-Jones substance: Vapor pressure (top), saturated densities (middle) and interfacial tension (bottom). Symbols indicate molecular simulation results.<ref name="Stephan e1699185">{{cite journal |last1=Stephan |first1=Simon |last2=Hasse |first2=Hans |date=2020-06-01 |title=Influence of dispersive long-range interactions on properties of vapour–liquid equilibria and interfaces of binary Lennard-Jones mixtures |url=https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/00268976.2019.1699185 |journal=Molecular Physics |language=en |volume=118 |issue=9–10 |article-number=e1699185 |doi=10.1080/00268976.2019.1699185 |bibcode=2020MolPh.11899185S |s2cid=214174102 |issn=0026-8976}}</ref><ref name="Stephan-2019b"/> Lines indicate results from equation of state (and square gradient theory for the interfacial tension).<ref name="Stephan e1699185"/><ref name="Stephan-2020a"/>]]
Properties of the Lennard-Jones fluid have been studied extensively in the literature due to the outstanding importance of the Lennard-Jones potential in soft-matter physics and related fields.<ref name="Lennard-Jonesium"/> About 50 datasets of computer experiment data for the [[vapor–liquid equilibrium]] have been published to date.<ref name="Stephan-2019b"/> Furthermore, more than 35,000 data points at homogeneous fluid states have been published over the years and recently been compiled and assessed for outliers in an open access database.<ref name="Stephan-2019b"/>

The vapor–liquid equilibrium of the Lennard-Jones substance is presently known with a precision, i.e. mutual agreement of thermodynamically consistent data, of <math>\pm 1\%</math> for the vapor pressure, <math>\pm 0.2\%</math> for the saturated liquid density, <math>\pm 1\%</math> for the saturated vapor density, <math>\pm 0.75\%</math> for the enthalpy of vaporization, and <math>\pm 4\%</math> for the [[surface tension]].<ref name="Stephan-2019b"/> This status quo can not be considered satisfactory considering the fact that statistical uncertainties usually reported for single data sets are significantly below the above stated values (even for far more complex molecular force fields).

Both phase equilibrium properties and homogeneous state properties at arbitrary density can in general only be obtained from molecular simulations, whereas virial coefficients can be computed directly from the Lennard-Jones potential.<ref name="Hill, Terrell L.-1956"/> Numerical data for the second and third virial coefficient is available in a wide temperature range.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Nicolas |first1=J.J. |last2=Gubbins |first2=K.E. |last3=Streett |first3=W.B. |last4=Tildesley |first4=D.J. |date=1979 |title=Equation of state for the Lennard-Jones fluid |url=https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/00268977900101051 |journal=Molecular Physics |language=en |volume=37 |issue=5 |pages=1429–1454 |doi=10.1080/00268977900101051 |bibcode=1979MolPh..37.1429N |issn=0026-8976|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref name="Stephan-2020b"/><ref name="Stephan-2019b"/> For higher virial coefficients (up to the sixteenth), the number of available data points decreases with increasing number of the virial coefficient.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Feng |first1=Chao |last2=Schultz |first2=Andrew J. |last3=Chaudhary |first3=Vipin |last4=Kofke |first4=David A. |date=2015-07-28 |title=Eighth to sixteenth virial coefficients of the Lennard-Jones model |journal=The Journal of Chemical Physics |language=en |volume=143 |issue=4 |page=044504 |doi=10.1063/1.4927339 |pmid=26233142 |bibcode=2015JChPh.143d4504F |issn=0021-9606|doi-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Schultz |first1=Andrew J. |last2=Kofke |first2=David A. |date=2009-11-10 |title=Sixth, seventh and eighth virial coefficients of the Lennard-Jones model |url=https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/00268970903267053 |journal=Molecular Physics |language=en |volume=107 |issue=21 |pages=2309–2318 |doi=10.1080/00268970903267053 |bibcode=2009MolPh.107.2309S |s2cid=94811614 |issn=0026-8976|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Also transport properties (viscosity, heat conductivity, and self diffusion coefficient) of the Lennard-Jones fluid have been studied,<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Bell |first1=Ian H. |last2=Messerly |first2=Richard |last3=Thol |first3=Monika |last4=Costigliola |first4=Lorenzo |last5=Dyre |first5=Jeppe C. |date=2019-07-25 |title=Modified Entropy Scaling of the Transport Properties of the Lennard-Jones Fluid |journal=The Journal of Physical Chemistry B |language=en |volume=123 |issue=29 |pages=6345–6363 |doi=10.1021/acs.jpcb.9b05808 |issn=1520-6106 |pmc=7147083 |pmid=31241958}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Lautenschlaeger |first1=Martin P. |last2=Hasse |first2=Hans |date=2019 |title=Transport properties of the Lennard-Jones truncated and shifted fluid from non-equilibrium molecular dynamics simulations |journal=Fluid Phase Equilibria |language=en |volume=482 |pages=38–47 |doi=10.1016/j.fluid.2018.10.019 |bibcode=2019FlPEq.482...38L |s2cid=106113718 |url=https://osf.io/67w4u/|url-access=subscription }}</ref> but the database is significantly less dense than for homogeneous equilibrium properties like <math>pvT</math> – or internal energy data. Moreover, a large number of analytical models ([[equation of state|equations of state]]) have been developed for the description of the Lennard-Jones fluid (see below for details).

===== Properties of the Lennard-Jones solid =====
The database and knowledge for the Lennard-Jones solid is significantly poorer than for the fluid phases. It was realized early that the interactions in solid phases should not be approximated to be pair-wise additive – especially for metals.<ref name="Zhen-1983">{{cite journal |last1=Zhen |first1=Shu |last2=Davies |first2=G. J. |date=1983-08-16 |title=Calculation of the Lennard-Jonesn–m potential energy parameters for metals |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1002/pssa.2210780226 |journal=Physica Status Solidi A |language=de |volume=78 |issue=2 |pages=595–605 |bibcode=1983PSSAR..78..595Z |doi=10.1002/pssa.2210780226|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref name="Halicioglu-1975">{{cite journal |last1=Halicioglu |first1=T. |last2=Pound |first2=G. M. |date=1975-08-16 |title=Calculation of potential energy parameters form crystalline state properties |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1002/pssa.2210300223 |journal=Physica Status Solidi A |language=en |volume=30 |issue=2 |pages=619–623 |bibcode=1975PSSAR..30..619H |doi=10.1002/pssa.2210300223|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

Nevertheless, the Lennard-Jones potential is used in solid-state physics due to its simplicity and computational efficiency. Hence, the basic properties of the solid phases and the solid–fluid phase equilibria have been investigated several times, e.g. Refs.<ref name="Köster-2017"/><ref name="Schultz-2018"/><ref name="Schultz-2020"/><ref name="Travesset-2014">{{cite journal |last=Travesset |first=Alex |date=2014-10-28 |title=Phase diagram of power law and Lennard-Jones systems: Crystal phases |url=https://aip.scitation.org/doi/10.1063/1.4898371 |journal=The Journal of Chemical Physics |language=en |volume=141 |issue=16 |page=164501 |doi=10.1063/1.4898371 |pmid=25362319 |bibcode=2014JChPh.141p4501T |issn=0021-9606|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Hansen |first1=Jean-Pierre |last2=Verlet |first2=Loup |date=1969-08-05 |title=Phase Transitions of the Lennard-Jones System |url=https://journals.aps.org/pr/abstract/10.1103/PhysRev.184.151 |journal=Physical Review |language=en |volume=184 |issue=1 |pages=151–161 |doi=10.1103/PhysRev.184.151 |bibcode=1969PhRv..184..151H |issn=0031-899X|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref name="Agrawal-1995"/>

The Lennard-Jones substance form fcc (face centered cubic), hcp (hexagonal close-packed) and other close-packed polytype [[crystal structure|lattices]] – depending on temperature and pressure, cf. figure above with phase diagram. At low temperature and up to moderate pressure, the hcp lattice is energetically favored and therefore the equilibrium structure. The fcc lattice structure is energetically favored at both high temperature and high pressure and therefore overall the equilibrium structure in a wider state range. The coexistence line between the fcc and hcp phase starts at <math>T=0</math> at approximately <math>p=878.5 \,\varepsilon\sigma^{-3}</math>, passes through a temperature maximum at approximately <math>T=0.4\,\varepsilon k_\mathrm{B}^{-1}</math>, and then ends on the vapor–solid phase boundary at approximately <math>T=0.32\,\varepsilon k_\mathrm{B}^{-1}</math>, which thereby forms a triple point.<ref name="Travesset-2014"/><ref name="Schultz-2018"/> Hence, only the fcc solid phase exhibits phase equilibria with the liquid and supercritical phase, cf. figure above with phase diagram.

The triple point of the two solid phases (fcc and hcp) and the vapor phase is reported to be located at:<ref name="Travesset-2014"/><ref name="Schultz-2018"/>

* <math>T_\mathrm{tr} = 0.32 \pm 0.001 \,\varepsilon k_\mathrm{B}^{-1}</math>
* <math>\rho_\mathrm{tr,gas} =..</math> not reported yet
* <math>\rho_\mathrm{tr,fcc} = 1.03859 \pm 0.0008 \,\sigma^{-3}</math>
* <math>\rho_\mathrm{tr,hcp} = 1.03861 \pm 0.0007 \,\sigma^{-3}</math>
* <math>p_\mathrm{tr} = 0.96 \cdot 10^{-9} \,\varepsilon\sigma^{-3}</math>

Note, that other and significantly differing values have also been reported in the literature. Hence, the database for the fcc-hcp–vapor triple point should be further solidified in the future.
[[File:LJ mixtures.png|class=skin-invert-image|left|thumb|440x440px|Vapor–liquid equilibria of binary Lennard-Jones mixtures. In all shown cases, component 2 is the more volatile component (enriching in the vapor phase). The units are given in <math>\varepsilon</math> and <math>\sigma</math> of component 1, which is the same in all four shown mixtures. The temperature is <math>T=0.92\,\varepsilon k_\mathrm{B}^{-1}</math>. Symbols are molecular simulation results and lines are results from an [[equation of state]]. Data taken from Ref.<ref name="Stephan e1699185"/>]]

==== Mixtures of Lennard-Jones substances ====
[[Mixture]]s of Lennard-Jones particles are mostly used as a prototype for the development of theories and methods of solutions, but also to study properties of solutions in general. This dates back to the fundamental work of conformal solution theory of [[Christopher Longuet-Higgins|Longuet-Higgins]]<ref>{{cite journal |last=Longuet-Higgins |first=H.C. |date=1951-02-07 |title=The statistical thermodynamics of multicomponent systems |url=https://royalsocietypublishing.org/doi/10.1098/rspa.1951.0028 |journal=Proceedings of the Royal Society of London. Series A. Mathematical and Physical Sciences |language=en |volume=205 |issue=1081 |pages=247–269 |doi=10.1098/rspa.1951.0028 |bibcode=1951RSPSA.205..247L |s2cid=202575459 |issn=0080-4630|url-access=subscription }}</ref> and Leland and [[John Shipley Rowlinson|Rowlinson]] and co-workers.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Leland |first1=T. W. |last2=Rowlinson |first2=J. S. |last3=Sather |first3=G. A. |date=1968 |title=Statistical thermodynamics of mixtures of molecules of different sizes |url=https://pubs.rsc.org/en/content/articlelanding/1968/TF/tf9686401447 |journal=Transactions of the Faraday Society |language=en |volume=64 |page=1447 |doi=10.1039/tf9686401447 |issn=0014-7672|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Mansoori |first1=G. Ali |last2=Leland |first2=Thomas W. |date=1972 |title=Statistical thermodynamics of mixtures. A new version for the theory of conformal solution |url=https://pubs.rsc.org/en/content/articlelanding/1972/F2/f29726800320 |journal=Journal of the Chemical Society, Faraday Transactions 2 |language=en |volume=68 |page=320 |doi=10.1039/f29726800320 |issn=0300-9238|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Those are today the basis of most theories for mixtures.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Rowlinson |first1=J.S. |title=Liquids and liquid mixtures |last2=Swinton |first2=F.L. |publisher=Butterworth |year=1982 |edition=Third |location=London}}</ref><ref name="Deiters-2012">{{cite book |last1=Deiters |first1=Ulrich K. |title=High-pressure fluid phase equilibria: phenomenology and computation |last2=Kraska |first2=Thomas |publisher=Elsevier |year=2012 |isbn=978-0-444-56354-5 |edition=1st |location=Amsterdam |oclc=787847134}}</ref>

Mixtures of two or more Lennard-Jones components are set up by changing at least one potential interaction parameter (<math>\varepsilon</math> or <math>\sigma</math>) of one of the components with respect to the other. For a binary mixture, this yields three types of pair interactions that are all modeled by the Lennard-Jones potential: 1-1, 2-2, and 1-2 interactions. For the cross interactions 1–2, additional assumptions are required for the specification of parameters <math>\varepsilon_\mathrm{12}</math> or <math>\sigma_\mathrm{12}</math> from <math>\varepsilon_\mathrm{11}</math>, <math>\sigma_\mathrm{11}</math> and <math>\varepsilon_\mathrm{22}</math>, <math>\sigma_\mathrm{22}</math>. Various choices (all more or less empirical and not rigorously based on physical arguments) can be used for these so-called combination rules.<ref name=Schnabel2007>{{cite journal |last1=Schnabel |first1=Thorsten |last2=Vrabec |first2=Jadran |last3=Hasse |first3=Hans |date=2007 |title=Unlike Lennard–Jones parameters for vapor–liquid equilibria |journal=Journal of Molecular Liquids |language=en |volume=135 |issue=1–3 |pages=170–178 |doi=10.1016/j.molliq.2006.12.024 |arxiv=0904.4436 |s2cid=16111477}}</ref> The most widely used<ref name=Schnabel2007/> combination rule is the one of [[Hendrik Lorentz|Lorentz]] and Berthelot<ref>{{cite journal |last=Lorentz |first=H. A. |date=1881 |title=Ueber die Anwendung des Satzes vom Virial in der kinetischen Theorie der Gase |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1002/andp.18812480110 |journal=Annalen der Physik |language=de |volume=248 |issue=1 |pages=127–136 |doi=10.1002/andp.18812480110 |bibcode=1881AnP...248..127L}}</ref>

<math display="block">\sigma_{12} = \eta_{12} \frac{\sigma_{11} + \sigma_{22}}{2} </math>

<math display="block">\varepsilon_{12} = \xi_{12} \sqrt{\varepsilon_{11} \varepsilon_{22}} </math>

The parameter <math>\xi_{12} </math> is an additional state-independent interaction parameter for the mixture. The parameter <math>\eta_{12} </math> is usually set to unity since the [[arithmetic mean]] can be considered physically plausible for the cross-interaction size parameter. The parameter <math>\xi_{12} </math> on the other hand is often used to adjust the [[geometric mean]] so as to reproduce the phase behavior of the model mixture. For analytical models, e.g. [[equation of state|equations of state]], the deviation parameter is usually written as <math>k_{12} = 1- \xi_{12} </math>. For <math>\xi_{12} > 1 </math>, the cross-interaction dispersion energy and accordingly the attractive force between unlike particles is intensified, and the attractive forces between unlike particles are diminished for <math>\xi_{12} < 1 </math>.

For Lennard-Jones mixtures, both fluid and solid [[phase rule|phase equilibria]] can be studied, i.e. [[vapor–liquid equilibrium|vapor–liquid]], [[liquid–liquid extraction|liquid–liquid]], gas–gas, solid–vapor, [[crystallization|solid–liquid]], and solid–solid. Accordingly, different types of [[triple point]]s (three-phase equilibria) and [[critical point (thermodynamics)|critical points]] can exist as well as different [[eutectic system|eutectic]] and [[azeotrope|azeotropic points]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=van Konynenburg |first1=P.H. |last2=Scott |first2=R.L. |date=1980-12-18 |title=Critical lines and phase equilibria in binary van der Waals mixtures |url=https://royalsocietypublishing.org/doi/10.1098/rsta.1980.0266 |journal=Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society of London. Series A, Mathematical and Physical Sciences |language=en |volume=298 |issue=1442 |pages=495–540 |doi=10.1098/rsta.1980.0266 |bibcode=1980RSPTA.298..495K |s2cid=122538015 |issn=0080-4614|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref name="Deiters-2012"/> Binary Lennard-Jones mixtures in the fluid region (various types of equilibria of liquid and gas phases)<ref name="Stephan e1699185"/><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Potoff |first1=Jeffrey J. |last2=Panagiotopoulos |first2=Athanassios Z. |date=1998-12-22 |title=Critical point and phase behavior of the pure fluid and a Lennard-Jones mixture |url=https://aip.scitation.org/doi/10.1063/1.477787 |journal=The Journal of Chemical Physics |language=en |volume=109 |issue=24 |pages=10914–10920 |doi=10.1063/1.477787 |bibcode=1998JChPh.10910914P |issn=0021-9606|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Protsenko |first1=Sergey P. |last2=Baidakov |first2=Vladimir G. |date=2016 |title=Binary Lennard-Jones mixtures with highly asymmetric interactions of the components. 1. Effect of the energy parameters on phase equilibria and properties of liquid–gas interfaces |journal=Fluid Phase Equilibria |language=en |volume=429 |pages=242–253 |doi=10.1016/j.fluid.2016.09.009|bibcode=2016FlPEq.429..242P }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Protsenko |first1=Sergey P. |last2=Baidakov |first2=Vladimir G. |last3=Bryukhanov |first3=Vasiliy M. |date=2016 |title=Binary Lennard-Jones mixtures with highly asymmetric interactions of the components. 2. Effect of the particle size on phase equilibria and properties of liquid–gas interfaces |journal=Fluid Phase Equilibria |language=en |volume=430 |pages=67–74 |doi=10.1016/j.fluid.2016.09.022|bibcode=2016FlPEq.430...67P }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Stephan |first1=Simon |last2=Hasse |first2=Hans |date=2020-01-23 |title=Molecular interactions at vapor–liquid interfaces: Binary mixtures of simple fluids |url=https://journals.aps.org/pre/abstract/10.1103/PhysRevE.101.012802 |journal=Physical Review E |language=en |volume=101 |issue=1 |article-number=012802 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevE.101.012802 |pmid=32069593 |bibcode=2020PhRvE.101a2802S |s2cid=211192904 |issn=2470-0045|url-access=subscription }}</ref> have been studied more comprehensively than phase equilibria comprising solid phases.<ref name="Lamm-2002">{{cite journal |last1=Lamm |first1=Monica H. |last2=Hall |first2=Carol K. |date=2002 |title=Equilibria between solid, liquid, and vapor phases in binary Lennard–Jones mixtures |journal=Fluid Phase Equilibria |language=en |volume=194-197 |pages=197–206 |doi=10.1016/S0378-3812(01)00650-1|bibcode=2002FlPEq.194..197L }}</ref><ref name="Lamm-2001">{{cite journal |last1=Lamm |first1=Monica H. |last2=Hall |first2=Carol K. |date=2001 |title=Monte Carlo simulations of complete phase diagrams for binary Lennard–Jones mixtures |journal=Fluid Phase Equilibria |language=en |volume=182 |issue=1–2 |pages=37–46 |doi=10.1016/S0378-3812(01)00378-8|bibcode=2001FlPEq.182...37L }}</ref><ref name="Hitchcock-1999">{{cite journal |last1=Hitchcock |first1=Monica R. |last2=Hall |first2=Carol K. |date=1999-06-15 |title=Solid–liquid phase equilibrium for binary Lennard-Jones mixtures |url=https://aip.scitation.org/doi/10.1063/1.479084 |journal=The Journal of Chemical Physics |language=en |volume=110 |issue=23 |pages=11433–11444 |doi=10.1063/1.479084 |bibcode=1999JChPh.11011433H |issn=0021-9606|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Jungblut |first1=Swetlana |author2-link=Christoph Dellago |last2=Dellago |first2=Christoph |date=2011-03-14 |title=Crystallization of a binary Lennard-Jones mixture |url=https://aip.scitation.org/doi/10.1063/1.3556664 |journal=The Journal of Chemical Physics |language=en |volume=134 |issue=10 |page=104501 |doi=10.1063/1.3556664 |pmid=21405169 |bibcode=2011JChPh.134j4501J |issn=0021-9606|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref name="Lamm-2004">{{cite journal |last1=Lamm |first1=Monica H. |last2=Hall |first2=Carol K. |date=2004 |title=Effect of pressure on the complete phase behavior of binary mixtures |journal=AIChE Journal |language=en |volume=50 |issue=1 |pages=215–225 |doi=10.1002/aic.10020 |bibcode=2004AIChE..50..215L |issn=0001-1541 |doi-access=free}}</ref> A large number of different Lennard-Jones mixtures have been studied in the literature. To date, no standard for such has been established. Usually, the binary interaction parameters and the two component parameters are chosen such that a mixture with properties convenient for a given task are obtained. Yet, this often makes comparisons tricky.

For the fluid phase behavior, mixtures exhibit practically ideal behavior (in the sense of [[Raoult's law]]) for <math>\xi_{12}=1
 </math>. For <math>\xi_{12}>1
 </math> attractive interactions prevail and the mixtures tend to form high-boiling azeotropes, i.e. a lower pressure than pure components' vapor pressures is required to stabilize the vapor–liquid equilibrium. For <math>\xi_{12}<1
 </math> repulsive interactions prevail and mixtures tend to form low-boiling azeotropes, i.e. a higher pressure than pure components' vapor pressures is required to stabilize the vapor–liquid equilibrium since the mean dispersive forces are decreased. Particularly low values of <math>\xi_{12}
 </math> furthermore will result in liquid–liquid miscibility gaps. Also various types of phase equilibria comprising solid phases have been studied in the literature, e.g. by [[Carol K. Hall|Carol]] and co-workers.<ref name="Hitchcock-1999"/><ref name="Lamm-2004"/><ref name="Lamm-2001"/><ref name="Lamm-2002"/> Also, cases exist where the solid phase boundaries interrupt fluid phase equilibria. However, for phase equilibria that comprise solid phases, the amount of published data is sparse.

==== Equations of state ====
A large number of [[equation of state|equations of state]] (EOS) for the Lennard-Jones potential/ substance have been proposed since its characterization and evaluation became available with the first computer simulations.<ref name="Metropolis-1953">{{cite journal |last1=Metropolis |first1=Nicholas |last2=Rosenbluth |first2=Arianna W. |last3=Rosenbluth |first3=Marshall N. |last4=Teller |first4=Augusta H. |last5=Teller |first5=Edward |date=1953 |title=Equation of State Calculations by Fast Computing Machines |url=https://aip.scitation.org/doi/10.1063/1.1699114 |journal=The Journal of Chemical Physics |language=en |volume=21 |issue=6 |pages=1087–1092 |doi=10.1063/1.1699114 |bibcode=1953JChPh..21.1087M |osti=4390578 |s2cid=1046577 |issn=0021-9606|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Due to the fundamental importance of the Lennard-Jones potential, most currently available molecular-based EOS are built around the Lennard-Jones fluid. They have been comprehensively reviewed by Stephan et al.<ref name="Stephan-2020a">{{cite journal |last1=Stephan |first1=Simon |last2=Staubach |first2=Jens |last3=Hasse |first3=Hans |date=2020 |title=Review and comparison of equations of state for the Lennard-Jones fluid |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/343378915 |journal=Fluid Phase Equilibria |language=en |volume=523 |article-number=112772 |doi=10.1016/j.fluid.2020.112772 |bibcode=2020FlPEq.52312772S |s2cid=224844789 |via=}}</ref><ref name="Stephan-2020b">{{cite journal |last1=Stephan |first1=Simon |last2=Deiters |first2=Ulrich K. |date=2020-08-20 |title=Characteristic Curves of the Lennard-Jones Fluid |journal=International Journal of Thermophysics |language=en |volume=41 |issue=10 |page=147 |doi=10.1007/s10765-020-02721-9 |issn=1572-9567 |pmc=7441092 |pmid=32863513 |bibcode=2020IJT....41..147S}}</ref>

Equations of state for the Lennard-Jones fluid are of particular importance in [[soft matter|soft-matter physics]] and [[physical chemistry]], used as starting point for the development of EOS for complex fluids, e.g. [[polymer]]s and associating fluids. The monomer units of these models are usually directly adapted from Lennard-Jones EOS as a building block, e.g. the PHC EOS,<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Cotterman |first1=R. L. |last2=Prausnitz |first2=J. M. |date=1986 |title=Molecular thermodynamics for fluids at low and high densities. Part II: Phase equilibria for mixtures containing components with large differences in molecular size or potential energy |url=https://aiche.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1002/aic.690321105 |journal=AIChE Journal |language=en |volume=32 |issue=11 |pages=1799–1812 |doi=10.1002/aic.690321105 |bibcode=1986AIChE..32.1799C |s2cid=96417239 |issn=0001-1541|url-access=subscription }}</ref> the BACKONE EOS,<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Müller |first1=Andreas |last2=Winkelmann |first2=Jochen |last3=Fischer |first3=Johann |date=1996 |title=Backone family of equations of state: 1. Nonpolar and polar pure fluids |url=https://aiche.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1002/aic.690420423 |journal=AIChE Journal |language=en |volume=42 |issue=4 |pages=1116–1126 |doi=10.1002/aic.690420423 |bibcode=1996AIChE..42.1116M |issn=0001-1541|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Weingerl |first1=Ulrike |last2=Wendland |first2=Martin |last3=Fischer |first3=Johann |last4=Müller |first4=Andreas |last5=Winkelmann |first5=Jochen |date=2001 |title=Backone family of equations of state: 2.
