More than 30 Lennard-Jones EOS have been proposed in the literature. A comprehensive evaluation<ref name="Stephan-2020a"/><ref name="Stephan-2020b"/> of such EOS showed that several EOS<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Mecke |first1=M. |last2=Müller |first2=A. |last3=Winkelmann |first3=J. |last4=Vrabec |first4=J. |last5=Fischer |first5=J. |last6=Span |first6=R. |last7=Wagner |first7=W. |date=1996-03-01 |title=An accurate Van der Waals-type equation of state for the Lennard-Jones fluid |url=https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/BF01443399 |journal=International Journal of Thermophysics |language=en |volume=17 |issue=2 |pages=391–404 |doi=10.1007/BF01443399 |bibcode=1996IJT....17..391M |s2cid=123304062 |issn=1572-9567|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref name="Kolafa-1994">{{cite journal |last1=Kolafa |first1=Jiří |last2=Nezbeda |first2=Ivo |date=1994 |title=The Lennard-Jones fluid: an accurate analytic and theoretically-based equation of state |journal=Fluid Phase Equilibria |language=en |volume=100 |pages=1–34 |doi=10.1016/0378-3812(94)80001-4|bibcode=1994FlPEq.100....1K }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Thol |first1=Monika |last2=Rutkai |first2=Gabor |last3=Köster |first3=Andreas |last4=Lustig |first4=Rolf |last5=Span |first5=Roland |last6=Vrabec |first6=Jadran |date=2016 |title=Equation of State for the Lennard-Jones Fluid |url=https://aip.scitation.org/doi/10.1063/1.4945000 |journal=Journal of Physical and Chemical Reference Data |language=en |volume=45 |issue=2 |page=023101 |doi=10.1063/1.4945000 |bibcode=2016JPCRD..45b3101T |issn=0047-2689|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last=Gottschalk |first=Matthias |date=2019-12-01 |title=An EOS for the Lennard-Jones fluid: A virial expansion approach |journal=AIP Advances |language=en |volume=9 |issue=12 |page=125206 |doi=10.1063/1.5119761 |bibcode=2019AIPA....9l5206G |issn=2158-3226 |doi-access=free}}</ref> describe the Lennard-Jones potential with good and similar accuracy, but none of them is outstanding. Three of those EOS show an unacceptable unphysical behavior in some fluid region, e.g. multiple van der Waals loops, while being elsewise reasonably precise. Only the Lennard-Jones EOS of Kolafa and Nezbeda<ref name="Kolafa-1994"/> was found to be robust and precise for most thermodynamic properties of the Lennard-Jones fluid.<ref name="Stephan-2020b"/><ref name="Stephan-2020a"/> Furthermore, the Lennard-Jones EOS of Johnson et al.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Johnson |first1=J. Karl |last2=Zollweg |first2=John A. |last3=Gubbins |first3=Keith E. |date=1993-02-20 |title=The Lennard-Jones equation of state revisited |url=https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/00268979300100411 |journal=Molecular Physics |language=en |volume=78 |issue=3 |pages=591–618 |doi=10.1080/00268979300100411 |bibcode=1993MolPh..78..591J |issn=0026-8976|url-access=subscription }}</ref> was found to be less precise for practically all available reference data<ref name="Stephan-2019b"/><ref name="Stephan-2020a"/> than the Kolafa and Nezbeda EOS.<ref name="Kolafa-1994"/>

=== Lennard-Jones potential as building block for force fields ===
The Lennard-Jones potential is extensively used for molecular modeling of real substances. There are essentially two ways the Lennard-Jones potential can be used for molecular modeling: (1) A real substance atom or molecule is modeled directly by the Lennard-Jones potential, which yields very good results for [[noble gas]]es and [[methane]], i.e. dispersively interacting spherical particles. In the case of methane, the molecule is assumed to be spherically symmetric and the hydrogen atoms are fused with the carbon atom to a common unit. This simplification can in general also be applied to more complex molecules, but yields usually poor results. (2) A real substance molecule is built of multiple Lennard-Jones interactions sites, which can be connected either by rigid bonds or flexible additional potentials (and eventually also consists of other potential types, e.g. partial charges). [[Molecular modelling|Molecular models]] (often referred to as '[[Force field (chemistry)|force fields]]') for practically all molecular and ionic particles can be constructed using this scheme for example for [[alkane]]s.

Upon using the first outlined approach, the molecular model has only the two parameters of the Lennard-Jones potential <math>\varepsilon</math> and <math>\sigma</math> that can be used for the fitting, e.g. <math>\varepsilon/k_\mathrm{B} = 120\,\mathrm{K}</math> and <math>\sigma = 0.34\,\mathrm{nm}</math> can be used for [[argon]]. Upon adjusting the model parameters {{mvar|ε}} and {{mvar|σ}} to real substance properties, the Lennard-Jones potential can be used to describe simple substance (like [[noble gas]]es) with good accuracy. Evidently, this approach is only a good approximation for spherical and simply dispersively interacting molecules and atoms. The direct use of the Lennard-Jones potential has the great advantage that simulation results and theories for the Lennard-Jones potential can be used directly. Hence, available results for the Lennard-Jones potential and substance can be directly scaled using the appropriate <math>\varepsilon</math> and <math>\sigma</math> (see reduced units). The Lennard-Jones potential parameters <math>\varepsilon</math> and <math>\sigma</math> can in general be fitted to any desired real substance property. In soft-matter physics, usually experimental data for the vapor–liquid phase equilibrium or the critical point are used for the parametrization; in solid-state physics, rather the compressibility, heat capacity or lattice constants are employed.<ref name="Zhen-1983" /><ref name="Halicioglu-1975" />

The second outlined approach of using the Lennard-Jones potential as a building block of elongated and complex molecules is far more sophisticated. [[molecular modelling|Molecular models]] are thereby tailor-made in a sense that simulation results are only applicable for that particular model. This development approach for molecular force fields is today mainly performed in [[soft matter|soft-matter physics]] and associated fields such as [[chemical engineering]], chemistry, and computational biology. A large number of [[force field (chemistry)|force fields]] are based on the Lennard-Jones potential, e.g. the [http://trappe.oit.umn.edu TraPPE force field],<ref name="Eggimann-2014">{{cite journal |last1=Eggimann |first1=Becky L. |last2=Sunnarborg |first2=Amara J. |last3=Stern |first3=Hudson D. |last4=Bliss |first4=Andrew P. |last5=Siepmann |first5=J. Ilja |date=2014-01-02 |title=An online parameter and property database for the TraPPE force field |url=https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/08927022.2013.842994 |journal=Molecular Simulation |language=en |volume=40 |issue=1–3 |pages=101–105 |doi=10.1080/08927022.2013.842994 |issn=0892-7022 |s2cid=95716947|url-access=subscription }}</ref> the OPLS force field,<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Jorgensen |first1=William L. |last2=Maxwell |first2=David S. |last3=Tirado-Rives |first3=Julian |date=January 1996 |title=Development and Testing of the OPLS All-Atom Force Field on Conformational Energetics and Properties of Organic Liquids |url=https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/ja9621760 |journal=Journal of the American Chemical Society |language=en |volume=118 |issue=45 |pages=11225–11236 |doi=10.1021/ja9621760 |bibcode=1996JAChS.11811225J |issn=0002-7863|url-access=subscription }}</ref> and the [https://molmod.boltzmann-zuse.de/ MolMod force field]<ref name="Stephan-2019a">{{cite journal |last1=Stephan |first1=Simon |last2=Horsch |first2=Martin T. |last3=Vrabec |first3=Jadran |last4=Hasse |first4=Hans |date=2019-07-03 |title=MolMod – an open access database of force fields for molecular simulations of fluids |url=https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/08927022.2019.1601191 |journal=Molecular Simulation |language=en |volume=45 |issue=10 |pages=806–814 |arxiv=1904.05206 |doi=10.1080/08927022.2019.1601191 |issn=0892-7022 |s2cid=119199372}}</ref> (an overview of [[force field (chemistry)|molecular force fields]] is out of the scope of the present article). For the state-of-the-art modeling of solid-state materials, more elaborate multi-body potentials (e.g. [[embedded atom model|EAM potentials]]<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Mendelev |first1=M. I. |last2=Han |first2=S. |last3=Srolovitz |first3=D. J. |last4=Ackland |first4=G. J. |last5=Sun |first5=D. Y. |last6=Asta |first6=M. |date=2003 |title=Development of new interatomic potentials appropriate for crystalline and liquid iron |url=https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/14786430310001613264 |journal=Philosophical Magazine |language=en |volume=83 |issue=35 |pages=3977–3994 |bibcode=2003PMag...83.3977A |doi=10.1080/14786430310001613264 |issn=1478-6435 |s2cid=4119718|url-access=subscription }}</ref>) are used.

The Lennard-Jones potential yields a good approximation of intermolecular interactions for many applications: The macroscopic properties computed using the Lennard-Jones potential are in good agreement with experimental data for simple substances like argon on one side and the potential function <math>V_\mathrm{LJ}(r)</math> is in fair agreement with results from [[quantum chemistry]] on the other side. The Lennard-Jones potential gives a good description of molecular interactions in [[fluid]] phases, whereas molecular interactions in solid phases are only roughly well described. This is mainly due to the fact that multi-body interactions play a significant role in solid phases, which are not comprised in the Lennard-Jones potential. Therefore, the Lennard-Jones potential is extensively used in [[soft matter|soft-matter physics]] and associated fields, whereas it is less frequently used in [[solid-state physics]]. Due to its simplicity, the Lennard-Jones potential is often used to describe the properties of gases and simple fluids and to model dispersive and repulsive interactions in [[molecular modelling|molecular models]]. It is especially accurate for [[noble gas]] atoms and [[methane]]. It is furthermore a good approximation for molecular interactions at long and short distances for neutral atoms and molecules. Therefore, the Lennard-Jones potential is very often used as a building block of [[molecular modelling|molecular models]] of complex molecules, e.g. [[alkane]]s or [[water]].<ref name="Eggimann-2014" /><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Abascal |first1=J. L. F. |last2=Vega |first2=C. |date=2005-12-15 |title=A general purpose model for the condensed phases of water: TIP4P/2005 |url=https://aip.scitation.org/doi/10.1063/1.2121687 |journal=The Journal of Chemical Physics |language=en |volume=123 |issue=23 |page=234505 |bibcode=2005JChPh.123w4505A |doi=10.1063/1.2121687 |issn=0021-9606 |pmid=16392929|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref name="Stephan-2019a" /> The Lennard-Jones potential can also be used to model the [[adsorption]] interactions at solid–fluid interfaces, i.e. [[physisorption]] or [[chemisorption]].

It is well accepted, that the main limitations of the Lennard-Jones potential lie in the fact the potential is a [[pair potential]] (does not cover multi-body interactions) and that the <math>1/r^{12}</math> exponent term is used for the repulsion. Results from quantum chemistry suggest that a higher exponent than 12 has to be used, i.e. a steeper potential. Furthermore, the Lennard-Jones potential has a limited flexibility, i.e. only the two model parameters <math>\varepsilon</math> and <math>\sigma</math> can be used for the fitting to describe a real substance.
